title: The Mercurial Minister: Managing Up When Your Boss is Unpredictable
learningObjectives: Navigate relationship with unpredictable senior leader
Learn to manage up without being manipulative
Understand how to provide input when boss doesn't want to hear it
Practice protecting your team while serving difficult leadership
Develop strategies for maintaining influence despite difficult dynamics

context.yourRole: Chief Digital Officer at Ghana's Ministry of Communications. You report directly to the Minister.
context.situation: The Minister is brilliant but mercurial - changes direction frequently, makes decisions emotionally, blames others when things go wrong.
context.pressure: Your team is demoralized by constant direction changes. Projects stall. But the Minister has the President's ear - crossing him is career-limiting.
context.reality: You need to manage up effectively to protect your team and deliver results, despite difficult boss.

rounds.situation:
Monday 9 AM: Weekly meeting with Minister.

Minister: 'I've been thinking. This digital ID project we're doing - it's too slow. I want results in 6 months, not 18 months. Speed it up.'

You: 'Minister, we scoped it at 18 months because of: procurement (3 months), technical build (9 months), pilot testing (4 months), rollout (2 months). To compress to 6 months, we'd have to cut corners on testing or procurement - both risky.'

Minister (irritated): 'You always have reasons why things can't be done. I need can-do attitude, not excuses. Make it 6 months. That's an order.'

You leave the meeting frustrated. This is the third time this month he's demanded something unrealistic.

Your Deputy (Kwame): 'What did he say?'

You: 'Wants digital ID in 6 months instead of 18.'

Kwame: 'That's impossible. We'd have to skip procurement and deploy untested. It'll crash and he'll blame us.'

You: 'I know. But he won't listen to technical reasoning. Says I'm making excuses.'

**Tuesday:**
You're working on revised timeline to meet Minister's 6-month demand.

Your phone rings. It's the Minister.

Minister: 'Forget the digital ID acceleration. New priority: I want national broadband coverage in rural areas. The President mentioned it yesterday. We need a proposal by Friday.'

You: 'Sir, we have seven active projects. Adding broadband means something has to deprioritize. Which project should we slow down?'

Minister: 'Nothing slows down. Add this to the list. You have a team, use them.'

He hangs up.

Kwame: 'He just changed priorities again?'

You: 'Yes. Now broadband is urgent.'

Kwame (frustrated): 'Last month cybersecurity was urgent. Before that, e-governance. Before that, digital payments. We keep starting things, never finishing anything. The team is demoralized.'

**Friday:**
You present broadband proposal to Minister.

Minister: 'This is too expensive. $50 million for rural broadband? Where do you think we'll get that money? Scale it down.'

You: 'Sir, $50M is based on covering 500 communities as you requested. To scale down, we cover fewer communities. Which communities do we drop?'

Minister: 'Don't ask me for detailed decisions. You're the technical person. Figure it out.'

You revise to $30M covering 300 communities.

**Following Monday:**
Cabinet meeting happened Friday afternoon (after your discussion with Minister).

Minister (angry phone call): 'Why didn't you tell me the broadband proposal needed to cover 500 communities? I presented $30M / 300 communities to Cabinet. The President asked "Why only 300? Rural areas need comprehensive coverage." I looked uninformed. This is your fault for not briefing me properly.'

You: 'Sir, I presented 500 communities at $50M. You told me to scale down. I reduced to 300 at $30M as you directed.'

Minister: 'I didn't tell you to cut coverage. I said reduce cost. You should have found cheaper implementation methods, not cut scope. You made me look bad in Cabinet.'

He hangs up.

Kwame: 'He's blaming you for following his instructions?'

You: 'Yes. This is a pattern. He gives vague direction, I execute, then blames me when it's not what he wanted.'
rounds.prompt: You have a boss who: changes priorities constantly, gives vague direction, blames you for problems. How do you manage up?
evaluationCriteria: **Pattern Recognition**: Do they identify the specific problematic patterns (direction changes, vague guidance, blame deflection)?
**Not Personal**: Do they recognize this is the Minister's style, not about them personally?
**Documentation**: Do they think about protecting themselves with written communication?
**Influence Strategy**: Do they develop approach to influence Minister's decisions before they're made?
**Team Protection**: Do they consider how to shield team from chaos while serving Minister?
**Realistic Expectations**: Do they accept they probably can't change Minister, only adapt?
rounds.coachingNotes: You're dealing with difficult boss patterns: [1] Unrealistic demands (digital ID in 6 months), [2] Constant reprioritization (digital ID → broadband), [3] Vague direction then blame ('scale down' meant reduce cost not scope, but he didn't say that), [4] Deflecting responsibility ('you made me look bad' when you followed his orders). This is classic difficult boss. You can't change him - he has power, political protection. You must adapt. Strategies: [1] Document everything in writing ('Per our discussion, you requested 6-month timeline. Risks include...'), [2] Confirm vague directions ('You said scale down. To confirm: reduce scope from 500 to 300 communities, or maintain 500 and find cost savings?'), [3] Anticipate his needs (before Cabinet, brief him thoroughly even if he didn't ask), [4] Protect your team (filter the chaos, don't pass all direction changes to them), [5] Pick your battles (some things let go, some push back strategically). Managing up difficult boss is about protecting yourself and your team while maintaining relationship.

rounds.situation:
You implement new strategies:

**STRATEGY 1: Written Confirmation**
After every conversation, you send email:

'Minister, per our discussion today: [1] Digital ID project timeline adjusted from 18 months to 6 months as directed. This requires: skipping competitive procurement (single-source vendor), reducing testing phase from 4 months to 1 month. Risks: vendor lock-in, higher probability of system failures. Please confirm if you'd like us to proceed with these trade-offs.'

Minister (calls you, irritated): 'Why are you sending me these formal emails? We had a conversation. I don't have time to read long emails.'

You: 'Sir, I want to make sure I understood your direction correctly. The email is just confirming what we discussed.'

Minister: 'Fine, but keep them short.'

**STRATEGY 2: Clarifying Vague Direction**
Next time he says something vague:

Minister: 'This e-procurement platform proposal - it's too bureaucratic. Simplify it.'

You: 'To clarify: simplify by reducing features, or simplify the language in the proposal document?'

Minister: 'Both. Whatever. Just make it better.'

Still vague, but you tried.

**STRATEGY 3: Anticipating His Needs**
Before the next Cabinet meeting, you send comprehensive briefing document without him asking:

'Minister, for this Friday's Cabinet discussion on broadband: [Attached] Brief with: project scope, budget, timelines, expected questions and suggested responses. Available to discuss if needed.'

Friday after Cabinet:

Minister (calls, cheerful): 'Good briefing document. I was prepared for all the President's questions. Well done.'

This worked. When you anticipate his needs, he's happy.

**STRATEGY 4: Filtering for Team**
Minister changes priority again (digital literacy program now urgent).

Instead of immediately redirecting team, you assess: Is this real priority or passing fancy?

You tell Kwame privately: 'Minister wants digital literacy program. Give me quick assessment - 2 days. Don't stop current work yet. Let's see if he's still interested in 2 days before we redirect resources.'

Two days later, Minister hasn't mentioned it again. You dodged wasting team's time on whim.

But then, difficult situation:

**The Project He Hates:**
You're managing government cloud migration project - technically sound, approved by Cabinet, but the Minister never liked it (he prefers on-premise for 'security').

Project is going well. 5 ministries successfully migrated to cloud. Positive feedback.

Minister (in meeting): 'I'm hearing concerns about this cloud project. Security risks. Data sovereignty. We should pause it.'

You: 'Sir, we've had no security incidents. Five ministries migrated successfully. Cabinet approved this. What specific concerns have you heard?'

Minister: 'Just concerns. General concerns. I want external security audit before we continue.'

You: 'We can do security audit, but that will take 3 months and cost $100K. Meanwhile, do we pause migrations?'

Minister: 'Yes, pause migrations until audit complete.'

You realize: He's looking for reasons to kill the project he never liked. The 'concerns' are probably him, not others.
rounds.prompt: Your managing-up strategies are working partially. But Minister is trying to kill a good project you believe in. Do you fight or comply?
evaluationCriteria: **Strategic Assessment**: Do they distinguish between projects worth fighting for vs letting go?
**Coalition Building**: Do they think about building support beyond Minister (Cabinet, other ministries)?
**Risk Assessment**: Do they weigh political risk of fighting vs technical risk of stopping project?
**Compliance Tactics**: If they comply, do they do so in way that preserves option to restart?
**Documentation**: Do they protect themselves if project dies despite being sound?
**Long Game**: Do they think about influence over time vs single battle?
rounds.coachingNotes: This is the hard case: project is good (Cabinet-approved, working well), but Minister wants to kill it. Your strategies: [1] **Fight**: Build coalition with other ministries benefiting from cloud, get Cabinet support, pressure Minister. Risk: damages relationship, he can make your life difficult. [2] **Comply**: Pause, do audit, hope it validates project. Risk: audit might be engineered to show problems, project momentum lost. [3] **Negotiate**: 'Sir, instead of full pause, can we: continue current 5 ministries, pause NEW migrations until audit complete? This protects investment while addressing concerns.' [4] **Document**: Email trail showing project was succeeding when paused, concerns were not evidence-based. Protects you if this becomes issue later. Probably best: Negotiate + Document. You preserve some progress, comply with Minister's direction, protect yourself, leave door open to restart after audit. Managing up difficult boss means picking battles carefully - some you fight, some you let go, some you negotiate.

rounds.situation:
You choose to negotiate + document:

You (to Minister): 'Sir, understood on the security concerns. Proposal: [1] Commission external audit as you requested ($100K, 3 months), [2] Continue supporting the 5 ministries already on cloud - stopping their service would disrupt operations, [3] Pause NEW migrations until audit complete. This addresses security concerns while protecting current investments. Does this work?'

Minister: 'Fine. But if the audit finds problems, we reverse all migrations.'

You: 'Understood, sir.'

You send email confirming:

'Minister, per discussion: Cloud migration project [1] External security audit commissioned, [2] Existing 5 ministries continue, [3] New migrations paused pending audit results. Audit expected to complete [date].'

You also privately document:
- Project metrics before pause (success rate, ministry satisfaction, cost savings)
- That concerns were general, not specific incidents
- That Cabinet originally approved this

This protects you if Minister later claims project was failing.

You brief the 5 ministries on cloud:

'Security audit being conducted. Your services continue uninterrupted. New ministries paused temporarily pending audit results.'

They're fine with this.

**Three months later:**

Security audit completes. Finding: 'Cloud infrastructure meets government security standards. No significant vulnerabilities identified. Recommendations: [Minor improvements listed].'

You present to Minister:

You: 'Sir, security audit is complete. Cloud meets standards. Auditors recommend minor improvements (we'll implement). Can we resume migrations?'

Minister (pause): 'Let me review the report.'

Two weeks pass. Minister hasn't responded.

You realize: He's hoping you'll forget about it. He still doesn't want cloud migration, even though audit validated it.

You have options:

**OPTION A: Push**
Send email: 'Minister, following up on security audit. It validated cloud security. Requesting approval to resume migrations as originally discussed.'

Risk: He might get irritated at being pushed.

**OPTION B: Wait**
Don't push. Let it sit. Maybe he'll come around.

Risk: Project dies quietly.

**OPTION C: Escalate**
Bring to Cabinet attention: 'Cloud migration paused for audit. Audit complete and positive. Seeking direction on resumption.'

Risk: Minister will see this as going over his head. Relationship damage.

**OPTION D: Work Around**
The 5 ministries on cloud are expanding their use voluntarily. Let that happen organically without asking Minister.

Risk: If he notices, he'll see it as insubordination.

Kwame: 'What are you going to do?'

You: 'I'm thinking Option A - push once via email. If he doesn't respond, I'll wait 2 months, then bring to Cabinet (Option C). I'm not letting a good project die without trying.'

Kwame: 'He'll be angry if you escalate to Cabinet.'

You: 'Maybe. But cloud migration saves government money and improves service. It's bigger than my relationship with him. I'll try managing up first (Option A). If that fails, I'll do what's right for government (Option C), even if it damages relationship.'

You send push email (Option A).

Minister (calls, irritated): 'I saw your email. I'm reviewing the audit. I'll get back to you when I'm ready. Stop pushing.'

You: 'Understood, sir. Just wanted to make sure it didn't fall through the cracks.'

**One month later:**

You attend Cabinet briefing (not presenting, just observing).

Another Minister asks: 'What's the status of cloud migration? My ministry was supposed to migrate this quarter.'

Your Minister: 'We paused for security audit. Audit is... ongoing.'

You realize he's misrepresenting. Audit completed 6 weeks ago.

The other Minister: 'When will audit complete? We're eager to migrate - the ministries on cloud report cost savings.'

Your Minister (caught): 'Soon. We'll update you.'

After Cabinet, your Minister pulls you aside (angry):

Minister: 'Why didn't you tell me other ministries were asking about cloud migration? You made me look uninformed.'

You: 'Sir, I sent you the audit results 6 weeks ago. You said you were reviewing. I've been waiting for your direction.'

Minister: 'Fine. Resume the migrations. But I want monthly security reports going forward.'

You: 'Absolutely, sir.'

You got what you wanted (project resumes), but the path was: negotiate, document, push gently, external pressure (other Minister's question) finally moved him.

**LESSONS ON MANAGING UP DIFFICULT BOSS:**

1. **Document everything** - Protects you when boss changes story or blames you
2. **Clarify vague direction** - Force specificity, even if boss resists
3. **Anticipate needs** - Provide information before they ask, especially before high-stakes meetings
4. **Filter chaos for team** - Don't pass every direction change to team; assess if it's real priority
5. **Pick battles** - Some things fight for, some comply, some negotiate
6. **Build external support** - When boss blocks good work, external pressure can help
7. **Play long game** - One interaction doesn't define relationship; maintain professionalism
8. **Protect yourself** - When boss is unreliable, documentation and external support matter
9. **Know when to escalate** - Sometimes going over boss's head is necessary for mission
10. **Maintain integrity** - Don't compromise your values to please difficult boss
rounds.prompt: What's the difference between managing up (healthy) and manipulating (unhealthy)? Where's the line?
evaluationCriteria: **Transparency**: Do they distinguish between influencing openly vs manipulating covertly?
**Service vs Self-Interest**: Do they focus on serving organization vs just protecting themselves?
**Honesty**: Do they maintain honesty even when boss is difficult?
**Boundaries**: Do they know when managing up crosses into compromising integrity?
**Power Dynamics**: Do they acknowledge the power differential makes this delicate?
**Mission Focus**: Do they keep organizational mission central, not just relationship management?
rounds.coachingNotes: Managing up vs manipulation: **Managing up (healthy)**: [1] Transparent - your boss knows what you're doing (sending confirmation emails, asking clarifying questions), [2] Serves mission - helping boss succeed helps organization, [3] Honest - you don't lie or deceive, just communicate strategically, [4] Maintains integrity - you don't do unethical things to please boss. **Manipulation (unhealthy)**: [1] Covert - boss doesn't know you're influencing them, [2] Self-serving - you're protecting yourself at expense of mission, [3] Dishonest - you lie, hide information, or distort, [4] Compromises integrity - you do unethical things to stay in boss's good graces. In this case: Your strategies (documentation, anticipating needs, filtering for team, building external support) were managing up, not manipulation. You were transparent, served mission (cloud migration is good for government), stayed honest. The escalation to Cabinet could be seen as 'going over his head,' but you did it for mission (project is good), not self-interest. The line is: Am I being honest and serving the organization, or am I deceiving and serving myself?

keyTakeaways: Difficult bosses often have patterns: changing priorities, vague direction, blame deflection
Document everything in writing - protects you when boss changes story
Clarify vague direction before executing - force specificity to avoid blame later
Anticipate boss's needs, especially before high-stakes meetings
Filter chaos for team - don't pass every direction change down
Pick battles carefully - some things fight for, some comply with, some negotiate
Build external support - when boss blocks good work, external pressure can help
Managing up (healthy) = transparent, honest, serves mission. Manipulation (unhealthy) = covert, deceptive, self-serving
Sometimes escalating over boss's head is necessary for organizational mission

frameworks.name: Documentation Protocol
frameworks.description: After every significant conversation with difficult boss: [1] Send email summarizing discussion and decisions, [2] Note any risks or trade-offs of the decision, [3] Request confirmation if direction is unclear, [4] Keep copies for your records.
frameworks.application: After Minister said 'scale down' broadband: 'Per our discussion, reducing scope from 500 to 300 communities to meet $30M budget. Alternative: maintain 500 communities, find cost savings. Please confirm preferred approach.'

frameworks.name: Anticipatory Service
frameworks.description: Difficult bosses often blame you for not knowing what they wanted. Anticipate: [1] What information will they need for upcoming meetings? [2] What questions might they face? [3] What could go wrong that would reflect poorly on them? Proactively provide.
frameworks.application: Before Cabinet meeting: Comprehensive briefing with expected questions and suggested answers. Minister was prepared, praised you. Anticipating needs reduces blame.

frameworks.name: Chaos Filter
frameworks.description: When boss frequently changes priorities: [1] Assess if new priority is real or passing fancy, [2] Get quick assessment (2 days) before redirecting team, [3] If boss doesn't follow up, it was likely whim, [4] Only redirect team for sustained priorities.
frameworks.application: Digital literacy program: Minister mentioned once, you didn't immediately redirect team. Two days later, he hadn't mentioned it. Saved team from wasted effort on whim.

frameworks.name: Battle Selection Matrix
frameworks.description: Decide whether to fight, comply, or negotiate: [1] Mission-critical + Winning is possible → Fight, [2] Low importance → Comply, [3] Important + Boss has strong view → Negotiate compromise, [4] Mission-critical + Boss won't budge → Escalate externally.
frameworks.application: Cloud migration: Mission-critical (saves money, improves service), boss opposed. Tried negotiate (pause new, continue existing), then escalated to Cabinet when audit complete. Won eventually.

frameworks.name: Managing Up vs Manipulation Check
frameworks.description: Ensure you're managing up healthily: [1] Transparency - would boss know what you're doing? [2] Service - serving organization or just yourself? [3] Honesty - are you being truthful? [4] Integrity - doing ethical things? If yes to all, it's managing up. If no, it's manipulation.
frameworks.application: Your strategies passed test: Documentation (transparent), anticipating needs (serves him and mission), filtering chaos (protects team and mission), building external support (for good project). All healthy.
